title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench (study_id=rX4f7-1), a paired comparison of a one‑shot NL→configuration pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline using the requested model gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and Mininet‑style emulation. The preregistered primary estimand was the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) under a binary episode success rule (validator accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback). Of 1,200 planned paired tasks we obtained 1,199 complete pairs. Baseline successes = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149); guarded successes = 1,199/1,199 (1.0). The observed paired difference = 0.002502085070892446; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957] (bootstrap_seed=1729, 10,000 resamples). Repair was invoked three times. The preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory breakdown (H3) was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup analysis and therefore is not present among the archived confirmatory artifacts; we disclose this omission and point readers to the archived analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json, execution/execution_manifest.json) for the exact evidence. Under the supplied synthetic tasks, validator settings, and shared_initial_candidate design the guarded pipeline produced no statistically significant improvement on the preregistered metric; we document execution, analytic deviation (Wilcoxon → exact McNemar), and limitations to guide reproducible follow‑up sensitivity studies.

sections.introduction: LLMs are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent expressed in natural language into executable device configurations for NetOps. Prior surveys and system papers emphasize that operational reliability is a property of the whole orchestration stack (model + verifier + provenance + sandboxed execution) rather than the base LLM alone. Generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) architectures are a canonical mitigation strategy: an LLM proposes a candidate, an automated verifier enforces syntactic/semantic constraints, and an automated repair loop iterates when needed. However, there is limited preregistered, paired evidence that quantifies whether verifier scaffolding yields operationally meaningful gains (rollback‑aware binary success) versus one‑shot generation under controlled, replayable conditions. We address this gap with NetOpsTraceBench (rX4f7-1), a preregistered paired benchmark comparing (A) one‑shot NL→config generation and (B) a guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline across 1,200 operator‑intent tasks in two simulated topology clusters (edge/core). The study’s primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Contributions: (1) a preregistered, artifact‑rich paired experiment and full execution artifacts; (2) a confirmatory paired analysis on 1,199 completed pairs with exact paired inference and bootstrap CI; (3) transparent reporting of an analytic deviation and of the preregistration item (H3) that was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup analysis.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and system proposals frame LLMs as components inside larger AIOps/NetOps workflows and call for workflow‑centered evaluation (trace quality, validator interactions, rollback semantics) rather than isolated one‑shot QA tests. Prior demonstrations of verifier‑assisted loops appear across NL→formal translations, topology compilation, and misconfiguration detection systems: these works show feasibility of generator+verifier patterns but typically evaluate on constructed or narrow held‑out sets and emphasize sensitivity to verifier rules and dataset difficulty. Studies of LLM failure modes (hallucination, semantic/unit errors, overconfidence, provenance loss, prompt‑injection) motivate guarded architectures because automated verifiers and provenance linkers can detect some but not all risks. The literature therefore motivates: (a) preregistered, workflow‑centered benchmarks that freeze analysis choices; (b) deterministic validators with explicit acceptance rules; and (c) archived provider and validator traces to enable reproducible interpretation. NetOpsTraceBench implements these recommendations by preregistering seeds, inclusion/exclusion rules, binary rollback‑aware success, and by archiving raw outputs and scoring artifacts.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and freeze: NetOpsTraceBench was preregistered (study_id = rX4f7-1; preregistration SHA‑256 = 77abe8b4...) and froze confirmatory hypotheses (H1–H3), inclusion/exclusion rules (contamination thresholds, parsing/execution failures), analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), seeds, stopping rules, and a power grid targeting a 5 percentage‑point MDE under baseline ≈0.70. The execution contract specified requested_model = gpt-5-mini, adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1, initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1, and generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (baseline and guarded share the same initial candidate per pair to isolate verifier/repair effects). Task corpus and validators: The corpus comprised 1,200 deterministically generated tasks (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) split into two simulated topology clusters (edge=600, core=600). Each task payload included initial_state, expected_final_state, explicit required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, workflow_policies, and a declared difficulty level. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 parsed candidates, enforced workflow policies, emitted validation_before/validation_after diagnostics (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes), and produced normalized_configuration strings. Binary episode success required (a) validation_after.valid == true, (b) emulator execution showing availability degradation ≤ preregistered tolerance, and (c) no automatic rollback event. Contamination and exclusions: Token/subsequence overlap T_contam=0.85 and optional embedding checks (cosine threshold 0.92) were preregistered; flagged pairs would be excluded automatically from the primary confirmatory analysis. Execution and analysis: The run obeyed stopping rules (max model calls = 2,400). The preregistered plan anticipated a nonparametric paired test and bootstrap CI; because outcomes are binary, the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant pairs plus a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000). Shared_initial_candidate design rationale: sharing the exact initial candidate between baseline and guarded isolates the verifier and repair mechanisms from generation variability—this reduces variance in paired comparisons but also reduces opportunities for the guarded pipeline to differ from baseline when the initial candidate already satisfies verifier rules. Preregistered but unexecuted confirmatory subgroup (H3): H3 specified a paired breakdown by topology cluster (edge vs core). The archived confirmatory analysis artifacts do not contain per‑cluster contingency tables or inferential outputs; thus H3 was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup analysis and remains unexecuted in the archived confirmatory artifacts (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv for the overall confirmatory evidence). This omission is disclosed here and in the Disclosure Statement; no new model runs or post‑hoc confirmatory tests were performed.
sections.results: Execution and accounting: The run completed 2,398 of 2,400 planned episodes producing 1,199 complete pairs (complete_pair_count = 1,199). Provider audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,202; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1; stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 1,200; repair = 3. Missingness: failed_baseline_episodes = 1; failed_guarded_episodes = 1; both_missing_pairs = 1. Primary paired outcome counts: contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) shows n11 = 1,196, n10 = 3 (guarded only), n01 = 0 (baseline only), n00 = 0. From these counts: baseline_success_count = 1,196/1,199 = 0.9974979149291076; guarded_success_count = 1,199/1,199 = 1.0; paired difference = 0.002502085070892446. Exact inference and CI: exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25 (archived in analysis/results.json). Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired difference = [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957], computed with bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Repair diagnostics: repair_stage calls = 3 and repair_applied = true in exactly three episodes; the majority of shared_initial_candidate outputs were accepted by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validation_after.valid = true and repair_applied = false for most episodes), which explains low repair invocation. Representative artifacts: execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json and representative task_manifest entries demonstrate heterogeneous declared difficulty levels and identical shared_initial_candidate contents for paired episodes; analysis/condition_summary.csv and execution/execution_manifest.json contain the full numeric accounting. Topology‑cluster confirmatory breakdown (H3) status: per preregistration H3 remained a confirmatory hypothesis, but the archived confirmatory analysis does not include per‑cluster confirmatory outputs. No per‑cluster contingency files or per‑cluster inferential results are present among the archived confirmatory artifacts; therefore H3 was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup analysis and is reported here as unexecuted (the overall confirmatory results above are the archived, executed evidence).
sections.discussion: Statistical interpretation: The observed discordant pattern (n10 = 3, n01 = 0) favored guarded but is too small in absolute count to reject the null under the prespecified thresholds (exact McNemar p = 0.25). The preregistered power plan targeted an MDE = 5 percentage points under baseline ≈0.70; the observed near‑ceiling baseline (≈0.9975) substantially reduced power to detect small absolute gains, which explains why a 0.25 percentage‑point increase is not statistically significant here. Operational interpretation: Two archived, artifact‑grounded mechanisms explain the null finding. First, the synthetic task generator plus explicit required_sequence fields produced tasks where the initial candidate often satisfied intent constraints, leaving little headroom for repair to improve a binary acceptance outcome. Second, the shared_initial_candidate design intentionally isolates verifier/repair effects but also constrains the space where the guarded pipeline can show differences from baseline when the initial candidate is already valid. Implications for benchmark design: To reveal conditions where verifier scaffolding matters, future experiments should (a) increase task ambiguity or adversariality, (b) vary verifier strictness and rule sets, (c) test multiple LLM families and fine‑tuned models, and (d) execute planned subgroup confirmatory analyses (e.g., topology clusters) when preregistered. Threats to validity: internal validity is strong for deterministic components (frozen seeds, automated exclusions), but construct validity depends on whether the binary success rule maps to operational risk tolerances; external validity is limited by single model family (gpt-5-mini), synthetic/consented tasks, vendor‑agnostic renderings, and Mininet‑style emulation that may not capture production vendor idiosyncrasies and convergence behaviors.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench and archived full provider, validator, and analysis artifacts. On 1,199 completed paired observations with gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5, the guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline yielded a small absolute improvement (≈0.25 percentage points) that was not statistically significant (exact McNemar p = 0.25; 95% bootstrap CI includes zero). Repair was invoked only three times under the chosen corpus and validator settings. We explicitly disclose that the preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory breakdown (H3) was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup analysis and is absent from archived confirmatory artifacts; follow‑up studies using more challenging or adversarial corpora, varied verifier strictness, and multi‑model comparisons are needed to determine conditions where verifier scaffolding produces operationally meaningful gains. All run artifacts and analysis code are archived to enable reproducible sensitivity studies.

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.

Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks and explicit required_sequence fields yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture vendor idiosyncrasies, routing convergence, and transient telemetry present in live deployments.

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness or rule sets could alter repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary. This deviation is recorded in archived analysis artifacts.

Preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory breakdown (H3) was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup analysis and is absent from archived confirmatory outputs; per‑cluster comparisons remain unexecuted in the archived confirmatory record.
